lessons.title: The Three Genres of Literature
lessons.content:
Literature is writing that shapes language imaginatively in order to explore human experience. CSEC English B asks you to respond to literature through three broad genres: prose, poetry and drama. Prose is written in sentences and paragraphs and includes novels, short stories, essays and biographies. It may be fiction (an invented story) or non-fiction (writing about real people, events and ideas). Poetry is written in lines and stanzas; it compresses meaning and relies on imagery, rhythm and sound to create feeling. Drama is written to be performed, so it is built from dialogue, characters and stage directions rather than from a narrator's voice.

Recognising the genre of a text is the first step in responding to it, because each genre works in its own way. In prose you watch how a narrator tells a story and how a character develops over time. In poetry you listen to the sound of the language and weigh the pictures the poet creates in a few carefully chosen words. In drama you must imagine the text on a stage, paying attention to what characters say and do, and to what the audience sees that the characters do not.

When you write about literature, name the genre and the technique you are discussing, then explain the effect the writer creates and how that effect supports the theme. A strong response never just retells the story; it argues a point about how the text works and why it matters.
objectives: Identify the three genres of literature and their key features
Distinguish between fiction and non-fiction prose
Explain how genre shapes the way a text is read

experiment.description: Genre Sorter: Match each text description to the genre it belongs to and the features that give it away.

lessons.title: Reading and Responding to Unseen Texts
lessons.content:
An unseen text is one you meet for the first time in the examination. You cannot memorise an answer for it, so the skill being tested is your method. Read the whole text once quickly to get the sense of it, then read the question and read the text again with the question in your mind. Mark words, images and details that seem important.

Questions on unseen texts usually ask for two kinds of meaning. Literal meaning is what the text says directly: a fact, an event, a description. Inferential meaning is what the text suggests without stating it: a character's feelings, the writer's attitude, or the mood of a scene. If a character slams a door and says nothing, the text does not tell you she is angry — you infer it from the action and the silence. Good readers move constantly between what is said and what is implied.

When you answer, use evidence. Quote a short phrase, or point to a specific detail, and then explain how that detail supports your answer. Answers that make a claim without evidence earn few marks, and answers that quote without explaining earn even fewer. The safest structure is point, evidence, explanation: state your idea, anchor it in the text, then say why it matters.
objectives: Apply a repeated reading method to an unseen text
Distinguish literal from inferential meaning
Support answers with short quotations and explanation

experiment.description: Main Idea Highlighter: Highlight the words in each passage that carry the main idea and the words that reveal how the character feels.

lessons.title: Subject, Theme and Message
lessons.content:
Students often confuse subject and theme. The subject of a text is what it is about — a short description of its content, such as 'a family struggling after a hurricane' or 'a boy's first day at a new school'. The theme is the idea the text explores through that subject, such as resilience, loss, ambition, justice, identity or the conflict between tradition and change. A theme is usually expressed as an idea, not an event.

A text may carry more than one theme, and themes often overlap. In a story about migration, for example, the themes might be hope, sacrifice and the meaning of home. The message or the writer's purpose is what the text seems to be saying about the theme: that sacrifice can strengthen a family, or that home is built from people rather than places. Writers rarely state a message directly — they build it through what happens, what characters learn, and the images and language they use.

To write confidently about theme, test your idea against the whole text. A theme you can support from several parts of the text — the opening, the climax and the ending — is far more convincing than one built on a single scene. And always link theme back to technique: how does the writer make you feel this idea rather than simply telling you about it?
objectives: Distinguish subject, theme and message
Identify more than one theme in a text and support it with evidence
Link theme to the writer's techniques and purpose

experiment.description: Theme Matcher: Match each subject to the theme it most naturally explores, then match the theme to a supporting detail.

lessons.title: Poetic Devices and Figurative Language
lessons.content:
Poets compress meaning, so a single image can carry several ideas at once. Figurative language is language used beyond its literal sense. A simile compares using like or as ('her voice was like gravel on a road'). A metaphor states that one thing is another ('the classroom was a beehive'). Personification gives human qualities to objects or ideas ('the mango tree stretched its arms across the yard'). Hyperbole exaggerates for effect, and oxymoron places opposites together to startle the reader.

Sound devices work alongside images. Alliteration repeats initial consonant sounds, assonance repeats vowel sounds, and onomatopoeia uses words that imitate sound ('crash', 'hiss', 'clatter'). Repetition and refrain create rhythm and emphasis. These devices are not decoration: they control pace, mood and the reader's attention, and Caribbean poets often use them to echo the cadences of nation language and oral storytelling.

When you analyse a device, never stop at naming it. Complete the chain: identify the device, quote it, state what picture or feeling it creates, and link that effect to the theme. 'The poet uses a simile' earns nothing; 'the simile comparing her voice to gravel suggests the hardship of her daily work, reinforcing the poem's theme of endurance' shows understanding.
objectives: Identify simile, metaphor, personification, hyperbole and oxymoron
Recognise sound devices and repetition
Explain the effect of a device and link it to theme

experiment.description: Device Detective: Match each quoted line to the device it uses, then decide which effect the device creates.

lessons.title: Sound, Rhythm and Form
lessons.content:
Rhythm in poetry is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables as you read aloud. Metre is a regular rhythm that repeats from line to line; free verse abandons that regularity in favour of the natural rhythms of speech. Rhyme is the repetition of end sounds, and a rhyme scheme (abab, abcb, for example) describes the pattern across a stanza. Not all poems rhyme, and a poem that begins with a fixed pattern may break it deliberately to signal a change in mood or thought.

Form matters too. A couplet is two lines, a quatrain is four, and a sonnet is fourteen lines, usually turning on an argument or a change of direction. A refrain is a line repeated at intervals, often at the end of stanzas, and enjambment is a sentence that runs past the end of a line, pushing the reader forward quickly. Caesura, a pause inside a line, slows the line down.

To discuss rhythm and form, read the poem aloud. Where does your voice speed up? Where does it pause? Which lines carry the repetition, and which break the pattern? Then explain what the pattern does: a broken rhyme scheme may suggest disorder, a repeated refrain may suggest grief that will not go away, and a long run-on line may mirror breathlessness or urgency.
objectives: Describe rhythm, metre, rhyme and rhyme scheme
Identify stanza forms, refrain, enjambment and caesura
Explain how sound and form shape meaning

experiment.description: Rhythm Lab: Drag each line into the stanza pattern it belongs to and label where the rhythm breaks.

lessons.title: Tone, Mood and Theme in Poetry
lessons.content:
Tone is the speaker's attitude towards the subject — admiring, bitter, wistful, angry, amused, reverent. Mood is the feeling the poem creates in the reader: calm, tense, sorrowful, hopeful. The two are closely related but not identical: a speaker may describe a scene with tenderness (tone) and leave the reader uneasy (mood). You detect tone through diction, imagery and the sounds the poet chooses, and you detect mood through the atmosphere those choices build.

Diction is word choice. A poem that calls the sea 'the ocean' sounds different from one that calls it 'the drink' or 'the grave'. Connotation — the feelings a word carries beyond its dictionary meaning — does much of the work in poetry. Because poems are short, every word is load-bearing: a change of one adjective can turn a tender poem into a bitter one.

Comparisons of two poems are common in examinations. Choose a clear basis for comparison such as theme, tone or the treatment of a place, and organise your essay around that basis rather than describing one poem and then the other. Use connectives — 'whereas', 'similarly', 'in contrast' — so that your essay moves between the poems all the way through, and quote both.
objectives: Distinguish tone from mood
Explain how diction and connotation create tone
Compare two poems using a clear common basis

experiment.description: Tone Deck: Flip through tone words, then match each tone to the diction that would create it in a poem.

lessons.title: Elements of Drama
lessons.content:
A play is written to be performed, so drama is built from different materials than prose fiction. Dialogue is what characters say to each other; monologue is a long speech by one character. Stage directions are the playwright's instructions about movement, props, lighting, sound and setting, and they are part of the text, not decoration — an entrance, a slammed door or a lit lamp can carry meaning as strongly as a line of dialogue.

Dramatic structure follows the same broad arc as fiction: exposition introduces the situation and characters, rising action builds complications, the climax is the point of greatest tension, falling action releases it, and the resolution settles the outcome. Because a play has no narrator, the audience learns about characters through what they say, what they do and what others say about them.

Setting in drama is more than a place name. It includes the period, the social world of the characters and the stage space itself — the house, the verandah, the yard. A playwright chooses a setting because it makes certain conflicts possible: a small island community where everyone knows everyone, a plantation yard, a city office. When you write about drama, always imagine the stage and ask what the audience would see and hear.
objectives: Identify dialogue, monologue and stage directions
Trace dramatic structure from exposition to resolution
Explain how setting creates possibilities for conflict

experiment.description: Stage Builder: Drag each element of drama to the part of the play it controls — action, character, or staging.

lessons.title: Dramatic Techniques and Conflict
lessons.content:
Conflict is the engine of drama. It may be internal (a character at war with herself), between characters (family against family), between a character and society, or between characters and nature or fate. A play usually carries several conflicts at once, with one dominating the main plot and others running through subplots.

Playwrights use techniques that are possible only on stage. A soliloquy lets a character speak her thoughts aloud while alone, giving the audience privileged access to her mind. An aside is a brief remark to the audience that other characters do not hear. Dramatic irony occurs when the audience knows something a character does not, which creates tension or pity. Foreshadowing plants hints of what is to come, and dramatic juxtaposition places two scenes side by side so that each comments on the other.

To write about technique, explain what the audience gains. A soliloquy reveals motive; dramatic irony makes the audience complicit or anxious; a withheld entrance delays a revelation and builds suspense. Then link the technique to theme: for instance, dramatic irony can expose how narrow-minded a community is, or how a character's pride blinds him to the truth everyone else already sees.
objectives: Classify internal and external conflict in a play
Explain soliloquy, aside, dramatic irony and foreshadowing
Link dramatic technique to the audience's response and to theme

experiment.description: Technique Table: Match each dramatic technique to the moment it creates and the effect it has on the audience.

lessons.title: Character, Motivation and Theme in Drama
lessons.content:
Characters in drama are built from their choices. Motivation is the reason behind a character's actions — fear, love, ambition, duty, guilt, revenge or loyalty — and it is often revealed when a character is under pressure. A character who is generous when life is easy and selfish when it is hard tells you what the play believes about human nature.

Distinguish a flat, one-dimensional character from a rounded one who changes. A dynamic character develops across the play, and the change usually carries the theme: a proud man humbled, a timid girl finding her voice, an opportunist exposed. Foils — characters placed in contrast with each other — sharpen this by making the difference in values visible.

When you write an essay on a character, answer the question asked. If the question invites you to discuss how a character is presented, organise your essay around the techniques used: what she says, what she does, what others say about her and how she changes. If it asks whether we sympathise with her, take a position and defend it with evidence from several parts of the play, and consider the counter-argument before you conclude.
objectives: Explain character motivation from textual evidence
Distinguish flat from rounded and static from dynamic characters
Build an argument about a character using evidence from across the play

experiment.description: Motivation Match: Match each character's action to the motive that best explains it and defend your choice.

lessons.title: Plot, Conflict and Structure
lessons.content:
Plot is the sequence of events in a story; story is the order in which those events actually happened. A writer may begin in the middle of things, flash back to the past, or move between two time lines to control what the reader knows and when. Structure is the shape the writer gives the plot: linear, circular, framed by a story within a story, or broken into episodes that jump between times and places.

Most plots follow a familiar arc. The exposition establishes setting, character and situation. A complication or inciting incident disturbs the balance. Rising action builds conflict through a series of events. The climax is the moment of highest tension or the decisive choice. Falling action shows the consequences, and the resolution closes the story — though many modern Caribbean stories end open-ended, leaving the reader to judge.

Conflict in prose may be internal or external, and it is usually both. To write about plot well, avoid retelling the story. Select the turning points that matter to your argument, explain how the writer builds tension or withholds information, and connect the shape of the plot to theme: a circular structure, for example, may suggest that nothing changes for the characters, or that history repeats in a community.
objectives: Distinguish plot from story and identify narrative structure
Trace exposition, complication, climax and resolution
Explain how structure shapes the reader's understanding

experiment.description: Plot Arranger: Put the events of a short story into the order they happen in the story and in the order they happened in time.

lessons.title: Characterisation and Point of View
lessons.content:
Writers build characters directly and indirectly. Direct characterisation tells you what a character is like; indirect characterisation shows it through appearance, speech, action, thoughts and the reactions of other characters. Indirect methods are usually more powerful, because the reader draws the conclusion.

Point of view is the angle from which the story is told. A first-person narrator uses 'I' and can be unreliable, limited to what she knows or willing to mislead. A third-person limited narrator stays close to one character's thoughts. A third-person omniscient narrator moves freely between characters and knows everything, while an objective narrator reports only what can be seen and heard. The choice of narrator controls how much the reader knows and how much she is asked to judge.

A useful question in the examination is: how does the writer make us feel about this character? Answer it by analysing technique. Notice the adjectives attached to a character, the verbs of her actions, the imagery used about her, and the gap between what she says and what the reader understands. Then explain the effect: sympathy, distrust, admiration or unease. Always link that effect back to theme.
objectives: Distinguish direct from indirect characterisation
Identify first-person, third-person limited and omniscient narration
Explain how point of view shapes the reader's judgement

experiment.description: Voice Matcher: Match each extract to the narrative point of view it uses and the amount of knowledge it gives the reader.

lessons.title: Setting, Atmosphere and Symbolism
lessons.content:
Setting is the time and place of a story, but it is never neutral. A setting carries social meaning: a yard in a Jamaican village, a colonial-era plantation house, a crowded bus, a hurricane shelter. Writers choose setting to place their characters under particular pressures and to make certain conflicts inevitable.

Atmosphere is the feeling a setting creates, built through imagery, weather, light, colour, sound and smell. Pathetic fallacy is the technique of making the weather mirror human feeling — a storm at the moment of crisis, a still afternoon after a death. Because atmosphere prepares the reader, it can make an event feel hopeful, ominous or tragic before it happens.

A symbol is an object, place or action that stands for something beyond itself: a locked gate for exclusion, a seedsman's plant for survival, a calabash for endurance. Symbols gain meaning from repetition and from context, so track them through the text rather than reading one occurrence in isolation. When you discuss a symbol, state what it represents, show the evidence that supports your reading, and connect it to the theme.
objectives: Explain how setting carries social and emotional meaning
Identify atmosphere and pathetic fallacy
Interpret symbols using repeated textual evidence

experiment.description: Atmosphere Deck: Flip through atmosphere words, then choose the imagery that would create each mood in a story.

lessons.title: Purpose, Audience and Form in Non-Fiction
lessons.content:
Non-fiction prose deals with real people, events and ideas: newspaper reports, features, editorials, speeches, essays, letters, diaries, biographies and travel writing. Before you analyse a piece, establish three things: who wrote it, who it is for, and what it is trying to do. Purpose is usually one of four kinds — to inform, to explain, to persuade or to entertain — and many pieces combine them.

Audience shapes language. A report for a broadsheet newspaper addresses readers differently from an editorial in a student magazine or a speech to a village council. Register, vocabulary and sentence length all shift with audience, and a writer who misjudges the audience loses them. Form matters too: a letter has a salutation and a sign-off; a speech opens with an address; an editorial usually states its position in the first paragraph and defends it.

Structure in non-fiction is often argumentative. A writer may open with an anecdote to win attention, present a claim, support it with evidence or example, answer a counter-argument, and close with an appeal or a recommendation. Mapping that structure is a fast route to understanding the writer's purpose, and it gives you a ready-made plan for your own essays.
objectives: Establish purpose and audience for a non-fiction text
Recognise the conventions of common non-fiction forms
Map the structure of an argument

experiment.description: Argument Outliner: Arrange the moves of a non-fiction piece into the order a strong argument would follow.

lessons.title: Persuasive and Emotive Language
lessons.content:
Writers persuade by appealing to reason (logos), to character and trust (ethos) and to emotion (pathos). Rhetorical questions, repetition, the rule of three, and direct address pull the reader into the argument. Statistics, expert opinion and examples strengthen it; loaded adjectives and vivid imagery make it felt. Caribbean speeches and editorials often combine all three appeals, moving from data to anecdote to a stirring final call.

Emotive language is powerful and dangerous. Words such as 'plague', 'flood', 'invasion' or 'hero' carry connotations that push a reader towards a conclusion before the evidence has been weighed. Exaggeration (hyperbole), sarcasm and innuendo are also persuasive devices. Whereas a fact can be checked, an emotive word must be evaluated: ask whether the writer is using the feeling honestly or manipulating it.

To analyse persuasion, identify the claim, list the appeals and devices used, quote them, and judge how convincing they are. A strong answer distinguishes what the writer does from how well it works: 'the repetition of the word 'now' builds urgency, but the claim rests on a single anecdote, so the argument is emotionally forceful yet thin on evidence'.
objectives: Identify logos, ethos and pathos in a persuasive text
Recognise rhetorical questions, repetition and the rule of three
Evaluate the effect and fairness of emotive language

experiment.description: Persuasion Highlighter: Highlight the appeals to reason, trust and emotion in each speech extract, then rank them by strength.

lessons.title: Reading Non-Fiction Critically
lessons.content:
Critical reading means testing a text rather than absorbing it. Separate fact from opinion: a fact can be verified, while an opinion expresses a judgement. Separate the claim from the evidence, and check whether the evidence really supports the claim or merely sits beside it. Notice vague attribution — 'experts say', 'it is widely believed' — which gives an impression of authority without naming a source.

Consider bias and reliability. Every writer has a standpoint, and a standpoint is not a fault; the fault is hidden or distorted evidence. Ask who benefits from the reader believing the piece, what has been left out, whose voice is missing, and whether opposing views are represented fairly. In Caribbean contexts, writing about tourism, crime, education or migration is rarely neutral, and a critical reader notices which interests are served.

Reading critically also improves your own writing. When you can name the techniques other writers use to sound convincing, you can use them deliberately and honestly, and you can explain in an examination why a passage persuades. Practise the habit of annotating: underline claims, bracket evidence, and write a one-line summary in the margin. An annotated passage is a plan for an answer.
objectives: Distinguish fact from opinion and claim from evidence
Evaluate bias, reliability and missing viewpoints
Annotate a non-fiction passage to prepare an answer

experiment.description: Fact or Opinion: Sort each statement into fact, opinion or unverifiable claim, and note the evidence you would need.

lessons.title: Planning and Structuring a Literature Essay
lessons.content:
A literature essay is an argument, not a summary. Begin by unpacking the question: underline the key word (discuss, compare, how, why) and the focus of the question (character, theme, technique, setting). Then decide your position — the line of argument you will defend — and select three or four moments in the text that support it. Making your plan in the first five minutes of an examination question saves time later.

The standard structure is an introduction, a series of body paragraphs and a conclusion. Your introduction should name the text and the writer, restate the question in your own words, and state your argument. Each body paragraph should begin with a topic sentence that makes a point, then quote or describe evidence, then explain the effect and link back to the question. The conclusion should not repeat the introduction; it should state what your argument has shown.

Organise body paragraphs by idea, not by the order of events. Signpost your argument with connectives ('firstly', 'more significantly', 'however', 'therefore') so that the examiner can follow your thinking. Quality beats quantity: three well-developed points defended with evidence earn more than six points mentioned in passing.
objectives: Unpack an essay question and identify its focus
Plan a line of argument with supporting evidence
Structure an essay with introduction, developed body paragraphs and conclusion

experiment.description: Essay Outliner: Drag the moves of a literature essay into the order that builds the strongest argument.

lessons.title: Using Quotations and Evidence
lessons.content:
Evidence is what separates an opinion from an argument. Use short quotations — a few words, embedded in your own sentence — rather than long block quotations copied out. Introduce the quotation so that it reads smoothly: the writer describes the yard as 'a sea of grass', suggests a landscape that is both beautiful and unmanageable. Then explain what the words do.

The point-evidence-explanation structure keeps you honest. State the point you want to make, provide the evidence, then explain how the evidence supports the point. Explain the specific words, not just the general idea: why 'sea' rather than 'field'? What does the choice suggest about freedom, danger or scale? Analysis of diction, imagery and structure at the level of individual words is what moves an answer into the top band.

Paraphrasing is acceptable when you cannot recall the exact words, but it must be accurate and signalled: the writer implies that the yard is impossible to control. Never invent a quotation. If you cannot remember the exact wording, describe the moment precisely instead — examiners reward accurate knowledge of the text, not guesswork.
objectives: Embed short quotations smoothly into a sentence
Apply point-evidence-explanation to a paragraph
Use paraphrase accurately when quotation is not possible

experiment.description: Quote Fixer: Repair sentences where quotations are dropped in without introduction or explanation.

lessons.title: Writing Under Examination Conditions
lessons.content:
Examination writing is a performance under time pressure. Budget your time before you write: divide the minutes available by the number of questions, and keep a few minutes at the end for proofreading. For an essay question, allow about five minutes to plan, most of the time to write, and two or three minutes to check. Answering the question you were asked matters more than writing a beautiful answer to a different one.

Begin by answering the question directly, and keep returning to it in every paragraph. Use the command word to control your depth: 'state' needs a fact, 'describe' needs detail, 'explain' needs reasons, 'discuss' needs a balanced argument, and 'evaluate' needs a judgement supported by criteria. Show the examiner that you know the text by naming characters and moments precisely rather than vaguely.

Common pitfalls cost easy marks: retelling the plot, ignoring the second half of a two-part question, writing about a text you were not asked about, and leaving questions unanswered. Also proofread for the basics — consistent tense, correct spelling of characters' names and titles, and clear paragraphing. A clean, well-organised script reads as confident, and examiners mark what they can follow.
objectives: Allocate time across questions and leave room for proofreading
Answer precisely according to the command word
Avoid the common pitfalls that lose easy marks

experiment.description: Exam Coach: Work through exam-room scenarios and choose the best decision for planning, timing and answering.

lessons.title: Prescribed Drama: Twelfth Night
lessons.content:
Twelfth Night is the Shakespearean comedy prescribed for Paper 02 Section A. Viola, shipwrecked on the coast of Illyria and believing her twin brother Sebastian drowned, dresses as a young man, calls herself Cesario, and takes service with Duke Orsino. Orsino is in love with the Countess Olivia, who is in mourning and refuses him, so he sends Cesario to plead his cause. Olivia falls in love with the messenger instead. Meanwhile Olivia's household - her uncle Sir Toby Belch, the foolish Sir Andrew Aguecheek, the maid Maria and the jester Feste - takes revenge on the puritanical steward Malvolio by tricking him into believing that Olivia loves him. In the closing movement Sebastian arrives with the sea captain Antonio, the twins are mistaken for one another, a duel and an arrest follow, and the confusion is resolved when brother and sister finally stand side by side. Orsino marries Viola and Olivia marries Sebastian, while Malvolio leaves vowing revenge.

The play is built as a main plot and a subplot that comment on each other. The main plot explores love as a kind of self-deception: Orsino is in love with the idea of being in love, Olivia falls for a servant she believes is a man, and Viola must hide the love she feels for her master. The subplot turns the same theme into farce, as Malvolio's fantasy of marrying above his station is punished in a darkened room and Sir Toby's household becomes a world of misrule and appetite. Disguise is the engine of both plots. It creates dramatic irony, because the audience knows what the characters do not; it lets a servant speak truths that no servant could speak plainly; and it asks the audience to think about identity, gender and social rank.

In the examination you will answer a Type A question on this single text - 35 marks, of which 25 reward your knowledge and argument and 10 reward the quality of your expression. Prepare four things: a scene-by-scene map of the play; a character list that says what each one wants and what blocks them; a short list of scenes you know in real detail (the explanation of the shipwreck in Act 1, Olivia's first meeting with Cesario, the gulling of Malvolio, the duel and the final reveal); and 12-15 short quotations grouped under two or three themes such as disguise and identity, love and self-love, or misrule and social order. Answer the question that is asked, not the one you prepared: if the question is about Malvolio, do not spend a paragraph retelling the plot.
objectives: Summarise the main plot and the subplot of Twelfth Night
Explain how disguise and self-deception drive the comedy
Plan a Type A essay using scenes and short quotations as evidence

experiment.description: Twelfth Night in order: drag the beats of Viola's story into the sequence Shakespeare gives them.

lessons.title: Prescribed Drama: Anansi
lessons.content:
Anansi, by Alistair Campbell, is the second drama text you may be examined on in Paper 02 Section A. Its central figure comes out of the Akan trickster tradition: Anansi the spider, carried to the Caribbean in the folklore of enslaved Africans and kept alive there as the small creature who survives by his wits. A trickster hero poses a particular question for a student of drama, because the audience is invited to admire cleverness even when that cleverness costs somebody else. Your work on this play is to establish, scene by scene, how the playwright makes you laugh, where the laughter turns uncomfortable, and what the play finally asks you to think about survival, power and the community the trickster lives in.

Because Section A rewards what you know about the text, build your study map from the copy of the play you are taught: the text and your teacher's guidance are the authority for the details of scene, staging and wording. Use the method you would use for any prescribed drama. Read the whole play twice, once for the story and once with a pencil in your hand. Produce a one-page map that states in one line what happens in each scene and who wins and loses in it. List the characters with what each one wants and how Anansi out-manoeuvres them. Mark every moment where the audience knows something that a character does not. Note where the play draws on the folk tradition - music, dance, storytelling, direct address to the audience, simple staging. Then copy out 12-15 short quotations, grouped under themes you can defend, such as cleverness and survival, the trickster against authority, the cost of the trick, or community and its traditions.

The Section A question is Type A: it asks about this single text, and the 35 marks are split 25 for content and argument and 10 for expression. A strong answer takes a position in the introduction (for example, that Anansi's cleverness is presented as a survival skill rather than a virtue), supports it with named scenes and short quotations, and returns to that position in the conclusion. General praise of the character earns little; specific reference to what happens and how it is staged earns a great deal.
objectives: Explain the trickster tradition behind the play's central character
Build a scene map, character list and quotation bank from your own copy of the play
Answer a Section A question with named scenes, quotations and a line of argument

experiment.description: Reading a trickster play: match each part of your study map to the question about the play it answers.

lessons.title: Prescribed Poetry: Comparing Two Poems
lessons.content:
Paper 02 Section B is the poetry section, and it is a comparative question: you write one essay on two poems from the prescribed anthology. The question may name the pair, or it may give a theme and let you choose two poems that explore it, so the poems you can pair up are as important as the poems you know individually. The essay carries 35 marks - 25 for content and argument and 10 for expression - and the examiners are looking for a comparison, not two separate essays stapled together.

Build a fact file for every poem you study, on one card or one page: title and poet; the subject in a single sentence; the form (stanza shape, line lengths, rhyme); the voice (who speaks, and how close to the experience the speaker stands); four or five devices with the effect each one creates; the tone, and the places where it shifts; the theme or themes; two short quotations worth remembering; and links to other poems - what this one can usefully be compared with, and on what ground. Then group the cards into clusters such as childhood and memory, home, migration and belonging, love and loss, nature and time, or resistance and voice. A question that lets you choose your own pair becomes easy if you hold three clusters of three poems each.

Comparison is a technique you can practise. A comparative paragraph makes one point about both poems and holds them together all the way through it: both poets use the sea as an image of what cannot be controlled, but where the first poem trusts it, the second fears it. Use connectives that compare (both, similarly, whereas, in contrast, while) rather than a full stop and a fresh start. Plan four or five of these paragraphs before you write, and make the introduction state what your comparison will show.
objectives: Explain what the Paper 02 Section B comparative poetry essay requires
Build a poem fact file and sort your poems into theme clusters
Write comparative paragraphs that hold two poems together

experiment.description: The poem fact file: match each part of a poem's fact file to the planning question it answers.

lessons.title: Prescribed Novel: For the Life of Laetitia
lessons.content:
For the Life of Laetitia, by the Trinidadian writer Merle Hodge, is one of the novels you may choose for Paper 02 Section C. It belongs to a tradition of Caribbean novels about a child's schooling: the story follows a young girl growing up between the world of her family and the world of the classroom, and it asks what education does to a child, what it costs and what it promises. Novels of this kind are examined through character, relationship and theme rather than through plot alone, so build your preparation around people and pressures, not around a chapter-by-chapter retelling.

Prepare the novel the way you would prepare any long text you must know well. Make a chapter map in which each chapter gets one line: what happens, and what it shows. Then draw the relationships. Who takes care of Laetitia, who disappoints her, who expects something from her, and how do those expectations change as she moves between home and school? Track the narrator's voice, because a novel about a child's growing awareness is carried by how much the reader is allowed to understand at each stage. Collect the details of ordinary Caribbean life that the writer uses - the yard, the road to school, food, work, language - and ask what each one adds to the reader's sense of the family's circumstances. Finally keep 12-15 short quotations and a few chapter references, grouped under two or three themes you can argue about, such as education and opportunity, family and duty, poverty and pride, or identity and belonging.

Section C asks for one essay of 35 marks, 25 for content and argument and 10 for expression. On a single text that means a Type A question: how does the writer present a particular character, relationship or theme? The strongest answers begin with a claim, develop three or four points in the order that builds the argument, use short evidence and explain the effect of the writer's choice, and finish by answering the question directly. Do not retell the story; every sentence should be doing something with the evidence.
objectives: Describe the novel's central concerns and how Section C examines a single text
Build a chapter map, a relationship web and a quotation bank for the novel
Argue a claim about a character or theme using chapter-level evidence

experiment.description: Which question type? Sort each Section C question into Type A (a single novel) or Type B (two stories compared).

lessons.title: Prescribed Novel: Animal Farm
lessons.content:
Animal Farm, George Orwell's short novel of 1945, is the other prose-fiction option in Section C. It is an allegory: a story with two levels of meaning. On the surface it is about a farm whose animals drive out their human owner and try to run the farm themselves; underneath it is about how a revolution can be betrayed from inside, and it maps closely onto the history of the Soviet Union. Knowing the second level is what turns a summary into an answer.

The animals rebel after the old boar Old Major describes a world without human masters, and they set up Animalism on the promise that all animals are equal. The pigs, as the most literate animals, take the leadership. Napoleon and Snowball compete for control: Snowball plans the windmill and leads the defence of the farm, while Napoleon raises a litter of puppies that become his private guard, drives Snowball out with them, and then runs the farm by terror and persuasion. Squealer, the silver-tongued pig, rewrites events and revises the commandments as the pigs take the milk, the apples, the beer, the beds and finally the farmhouse. Boxer the cart-horse works himself to exhaustion rebuilding the windmill and is sold when he collapses. At the end the pigs play cards with the human farmers, and the animals looking in through the window cannot tell the pigs from the men. Read the animals as figures: Old Major is the visionary whose ideas outlive him, Napoleon is power that seizes and keeps control, Snowball is the rival whose achievements are erased from the record, Squealer is the propaganda that keeps the others believing, Boxer is the loyal worker who is spent, and Benjamin is the sceptic who understands everything and says nothing.

The novel's techniques are the real subject of the examination. The fable form keeps the story simple and the judgement sharp. The seven commandments work as a recurring motif, changing a word at a time to show how quickly a principle can be hollowed out while its wording survives - the final version, that all animals are equal but some are more equal than others, is the whole argument in one sentence. Irony is everywhere: the animals' hard-won freedom ends in a world harsher than the one they overthrew. Prepare chapter-level knowledge, a character-to-figure list and short quotations about power, language and work.
objectives: Explain the allegory and match the characters to what they represent
Analyse how propaganda and the rewriting of language control the animals
Plan a Section C essay on power, language or equality

experiment.description: Animal Farm: match each character to the force they represent in the allegory.

lessons.title: Prescribed Prose: Comparing Two Short Stories
lessons.content:
The alternative to a single novel in Section C is a comparative question on short stories: one essay on two stories from the prescribed anthology, again 35 marks, with 25 for content and argument and 10 for expression. The question may name two stories or ask you to choose stories that treat the same experience, so - exactly as in the poetry section - the pairs you can build matter as much as the individual stories you know.

A short story is a single effect: one conflict, one turning point, one ending, and the ending is usually where the meaning is decided. That is why comparative questions so often turn on how a story closes. Build a fact file for each story you prepare - title and writer, setting, who tells the story, the central conflict, the turning point, how it ends, the theme, three or four short quotations and the one technique the writer leans on - and then do what the examiners want: choose a shared focus and compare the two stories on it all the way through each paragraph. Prepare six to eight stories well rather than twelve badly, and arrange them in clusters (growing up, leaving home, family and duty, money and survival, loss) so that whatever the question asks, you already have a pair.

The most common way to lose marks is to summarise the first story, summarise the second, and add a closing sentence about them being similar. A comparative sentence holds both texts at once: in the first story the child's silence is loyalty, whereas in the second the same silence is fear. Practise turning a summary sentence into a comparative one; it is the single fastest improvement available in this section.
objectives: Explain what the Section C comparative short-story question requires
Build a story fact file and pair stories in theme clusters
Turn summary sentences into comparative sentences

experiment.description: Compare or summarise? Sort each sentence into one that compares two stories and one that summarises a single story.
